did_you_know.text: Psalm 127 opens with the heading “A Song of Ascents. Of Solomon,” so it is counted among the Songs of Ascents and bears Solomon’s name in its heading.
The verse presents two examples of human effort: building a house and guarding a city. In both cases, it emphasizes that work and watchfulness are not enough without the LORD’s help.
The word “vain” appears twice in the verse: the builders’ labor without the LORD is vain, and the watchman’s vigilance without the LORD’s protection is vain.
The verse describes people who rise early, stay up late, and eat “the bread of anxious toil”—an expression that conveys labor and worry.
The verse ends, “For he gives his beloved sleep.” The word “sleep” is related to rest, and the verse contrasts rest and sleep with labor and worry.
Children are called “a heritage from the LORD,” and “the fruit of the womb” is described as a reward. Thus, the psalm presents children as a gift from the LORD.

Children born in one’s youth are compared to “arrows in the hand of a warrior.” The image emphasizes their strength and the possibility that they will act in the future, like arrows sent toward a target.
The person whose quiver is filled with sons is called “blessed.” A quiver is used to carry arrows, so this continues the image of sons as arrows.
The ending mentions “the gate,” a place where public meetings and disputes took place. According to the verse, having many sons gives a father confidence when facing enemies there.
